Its central idea is the quality of being lifted up or distinguished, whether that prominence is rightly recognized or wrongly claimed.

Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

These passages connect Gerizim with God’s commands and with spoken declarations, showing its role as a recognized location within Israel’s history. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal lexical function is as the name Ophir.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “lap,” referring to the area or fold formed in front of a person. It occurs twice in the Old Testament, including Nehemiah 5:13 and Isaiah 49:22. As a noun, it identifies a physical place or part of the body rather than an action. Its use is closely associated with something being held, gathered, or positioned in the lap, while the precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Hebrew verb means “utterly,” describing an action carried out completely and without anything held back. It is used in the Old Testament for something being dealt with in a total way, rather than partially. The word occurs 52 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 48 verses. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word describes the act of making or gathering a “fire” or “heap.” Its meaning is connected with something being formed into a concentrated pile or burning mass, rather than with a general movement or feeling. It occurs four times in the Old Testament, in Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah. Because no short definition is recorded, these two repeated meaning terms provide the clearest ordinary sense available for understanding the word’s use.

This Hebrew word means "spotted" and describes something distinguished by visible spots or patches. The word occurs eight times in the Old Testament, with its clearest recurring sense preserved in the rendering "spotted." Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Jibsam is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Bible corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:2. Its specific significance therefore depends on the surrounding passage and its immediate context.

This Hebrew word means “howling.” It describes a loud, sustained cry rather than ordinary speech. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 32:10, and functions as a concrete description of the sound or cry being presented there. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but its basic sense remains a howling cry. This is a rare word in the Hebrew corpus, with no other recorded occurrence.

This Hebrew word describes something as perverse—turned away from what is right or proper. It functions as a predicate, stating a condition or quality rather than naming a person or object. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Numbers 22:32 and Job 16:11. e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Achsah,” referring to a woman named in the Old Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action word.
